question: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of right-sided weakness and subjective decreased sensation that started 30 minutes ago. The patient reports that his symptoms started to ease 5 minutes after onset and have now completely resolved. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. His current medications include lisinopril, metformin, and sitagliptin. He is 183 cm (6 ft 0 in) tall and weighs 105 kg (220 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. He appears well. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. Neurological examination shows no abnormalities. Cardiac examination shows regular rate and rhythm and a left-sided carotid bruit. Complete blood count, serum glucose, and electrolytes are within the reference ranges. An ECG shows sinus rhythm and left axis deviation. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows no abnormalities. Carotid doppler ultrasound shows 45% stenosis in the left carotid artery and 15% stenosis in the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Right-sided weakness and decreased sensation" -> "Transient ischemic attack (TIA)" -> "Risk factors: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, smoking" -> "Possible carotid artery disease" -> "Carotid doppler ultrasound findings: -> 45%
CHAIN: "Left-sided carotid bruit" -> "Indication of carotid artery disease" -> "Carotid doppler ultrasound findings: -> 45%
CHAIN: "No abnormalities on head CT scan" -> "Exclusion of acute intracranial pathology" -> "Focus on extracranial causes of symptoms" -> "Carotid doppler ultrasound findings: -> 45%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of right-sided weakness and decreased sensation, along with risk factors like hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and smoking, suggests a transient ischemic attack (TIA) with possible carotid artery disease. The carotid doppler ultrasound findings of 45% stenosis in the left carotid artery support this. Given the indication of carotid artery disease and the presence of a left-sided carotid bruit, the most appropriate next step in management would be antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of further TIA or stroke.
analysis: The patient's presentation, risk factors, and carotid doppler ultrasound findings strongly suggest a transient ischemic attack (TIA) with possible carotid artery disease. Given the indication of carotid artery disease and the presence of a left-sided carotid bruit, the most appropriate next step in management would be antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of further TIA or stroke. This aligns with the standard approach to managing TIA in the setting of carotid artery disease.
